nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio. For all integers $p, q, r$, the number $p + q + r$ is a term $p \lfloor n \varphi \rfloor + q n + r$, $n \ge 1$, of the generalized Beatty sequence $V(p, q, r)$; it is the term at $n = 1$, since $\lfloor \varphi \rfloor = 1$.

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $T$ be a finite set of integers with $T \subseteq [-2n, -1]$ and $-2n \in T$ that contains no two consecutive integers. Then there are a natural number $N$ and a base phi expansion $S$ of $N$ (the set of positions of its digits $1$) with $\{i \in S : i < 0\} = T$. In words, every Zeckendorf word of even length $2n \ge 2$ ending in $1$ is the negative part $\beta^-(N)$ of some $N$.

nodes.summary: For a finite set $S$ of integers, the base phi value of $S$ is the real number $\sum_{i \in S} \varphi^i$, where $\varphi = (1 + \sqrt 5)/2$ is the golden ratio. It is the number represented by the base phi expansion with digit $1$ at each position in $S$ and digit $0$ at every other position.
nodes.title: Value of a base phi expansion

nodes.summary: For integers $p$, $q$ and $r$, this is the set of integers $p \lfloor n\varphi \rfloor + qn + r$ for all natural numbers $n \ge 0$, where $\varphi$ is the golden ratio: the set of values $V(p, q, r)(n)$, $n \ge 0$, of the generalized Beatty sequence $V(p, q, r)$, which the paper denotes $V_0(p, q, r)$.
nodes.title: Terms of a generalized Beatty sequence from index zero

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio and, for integers $a$, $b$, $c$, let $V(a, b, c)$ be the set of integers $a \lfloor n\varphi \rfloor + bn + c$ for natural numbers $n \ge 1$. Let $p$, $q$, $r$ be integers with $p + q > 0$ and $2p + q > 0$. If $U$ and $W$ are disjoint sets of integers with $U \cup W = V(p, q, r)$ and $U = V(p + q, p, r - p)$, then $W = V(2p + q, p + q, r)$.
nodes.title: Complement of the lower Wythoff part of a generalized Beatty sequence

nodes.title: Terms of a generalized Beatty sequence

nodes.summary: Let $N$ and $n$ be natural numbers, let $S$ be a finite set of integers with no two consecutive elements (a Bergman expansion) whose base phi value is $N$, and let $R$ be the least element of $S$. Write $L_m$ for the $m$-th Lucas number. If $L_{2n} \le N \le L_{2n+1}$, then $-R = 2n$. If $L_{2n+1} + 1 \le N \le L_{2n+2} - 1$, then $-R = 2n + 2$.
nodes.title: Lowest Bergman digit of $N$ from its Lucas interval

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $k$ be a natural number with $k \le L_{2n-1}$, where $L_m$ is the $m$-th Lucas number. Let $S$ and $T$ be finite sets of integers, each with no two consecutive elements (Bergman expansions), whose base phi values are $k$ and $L_{2n} + k$ respectively. Then $2n \notin S$, $-2n \notin S$, and $T = S \cup \{2n, -2n\}$.
nodes.title: Bergman expansion of $L_{2n} + k$

nodes.summary: Let $n \ge 2$, let $k$ be a natural number, and write $L_m$ for the $m$-th Lucas number. Call a finite set of integers with no two consecutive elements a Bergman expansion. Let $S$ and $T$ be Bergman expansions, let $a$ and $t$ be the least and the greatest element of $S$, let $S' = S \setminus \{a, t\}$, and for an integer $c$ write $S' + c = \{x + c : x \in S'\}$.

If the base phi value of $S$ is $F_{2n}$, then $S = \{t + 4j : 0 \le j < n\}$ for some integer $t$. If the base phi value of $S$ is $F_{2n+1}$, then $S = \{t\} \cup \{t + 3 + 4j : 0 \le j < n\}$ for some integer $t$.

nodes.title: Lucas numbers from Fibonacci numbers

nodes.summary: Let $F_k$ be the Fibonacci numbers ($F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$) and $L_k$ the Lucas numbers ($L_0 = 2$, $L_1 = 1$). Call $\Lambda_{2n} = [L_{2n}, L_{2n+1}]$ the even Lucas interval and $\Lambda_{2n+1} = [L_{2n+1} + 1, L_{2n+2} - 1]$ the odd Lucas interval. For every $n \ge 1$, $F_{2n+2} \in \Lambda_{2n}$ and $F_{2n+3} \in \Lambda_{2n+1}$.
nodes.title: Fibonacci numbers in the Lucas intervals

nodes.summary: Let $F_i$ be the Fibonacci numbers ($F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$), and let $\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathrm{FIB}}(m)$ be the number of ways to write $m$ as a sum of Fibonacci numbers $F_i$ with distinct indices $i \ge 2$. Then $\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathrm{FIB}}(0), \dots, \mathrm{Tot}_{\mathrm{FIB}}(8)$ are $1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3$.
nodes.title: Small values of the Fibonacci representation count

nodes.summary: For a natural number $m$, $\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathrm{FIB}}(m)$ is the number of finite sets $T$ of indices $i \ge 2$ with $\sum_{i \in T} F_i = m$, where $F_i$ are the Fibonacci numbers ($F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$); that is, the number of ways to write $m$ as a sum of Fibonacci numbers with distinct indices at least $2$ (OEIS A000119). Indices above $m + 1$ never occur because $F_{m+2} > m$.

nodes.summary: Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio. A finite set $S$ of integers, read as the positions of the digits $1$ of a finite expansion with digits $0$ and $1$, is a base phi expansion of the natural number $N$ when it is a Bergman expansion (no two digits $1$ are adjacent: $i \in S$ implies $i + 1 \notin S$) and its value $\sum_{i \in S} \varphi^i$ equals $N$.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved

stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
